title: The Language of Remembrance
sub: Grades 5–8 · ELA · How words are built to be remembered
objective: Students will study how the exhibition’s words are built to be remembered: the **anaphora** of the film’s six title cards, the **rule of three** in *the eleventh hour, the eleventh day, the eleventh month*, the **careful words** a writer uses when a fact is uncertain, and the **formal register** of an epitaph, a proclamation and a promise. They will then write their own words of remembrance, using the devices and only true facts.

objectives.heading: By the end of this lesson you will be able to:
objectives.why: People remember the end of the Great War in a handful of words: eleven, silence, never forgotten. Those words were chosen and built with care, and a careful writer can learn how.

materials: The title cards and quotations on page 3, projected or printed
*When the Guns Fell Silent*, the exhibition’s short film, if you can play it
connection: **Online,** watch *When the Guns Fell Silent* and see the six cards appear one at a time, before the record and the silence. **In the exhibition,** hear the posters read aloud, and find the last line of each.

steps.title: Six cards
script: Show the six title cards from the exhibition’s short film, one line at a time, and have the class read them aloud together. *“Read the six cards aloud. What do you notice about how they are built?”* Students will hear the repeated *After*, the numbers growing, and the last card breaking the pattern. *“Writers build words like this on purpose. Today we find out how.”*

screen.text:
After 1,568 days of war.
After 20 million dead.
After boys lied about their age to fight.
After trenches stretched 475 miles across Europe.
After one final soldier fell at 10:59 AM.
The guns finally went silent.
screen.cite: The title cards of When the Guns Fell Silent

steps.purpose: Hear a pattern before naming it.
students: Read the six cards aloud. What do you notice about how they are built?
Why does the last card not begin with “After”?

steps.title: The eleventh hour
script: **Repetition and the rule of three.** Name the hook’s device: **anaphora**, the same word opening each line. Then read the poster’s last sentence. *Eleventh* comes three times, each time a bigger unit, hour, day, month, and then the sentence turns on **but**: the guns fell silent, *but our gratitude never will*. Ask what the contrast does.

screen.text: At the eleventh hour, on the eleventh day, of the eleventh month, the guns fell silent—but our gratitude never will.
screen.cite: When the Guns Fell Silent at the 11th Hour

steps.purpose: See repetition and the rule of three at work, and the turn on “but.”
students: What does “but” turn the sentence toward?

steps.title: Careful words
script: **Careful words.** Read the poster’s two passages about nicknames: *“They were called “doughboys,” possibly because the large brass buttons on their uniforms resembled small fried-dough pastries, or perhaps from the dust that coated infantry on the march in the Mexican-American War, as if they’d been rolled in flour. Whatever the origin, the nickname stuck.”* and *“They fought in decisive battles like Belleau Wood, where U.S. Marines fought so fiercely that legend says German soldiers called them “Devil Dogs.””* The writer does not know for sure, and says so. Compare these with the poster’s numbers, which are stated plainly. Careful writing tells the reader how sure to be.

screen.caption: Careful words on The Doughboys poster: the writer marks what is not certain

cells: They were called “doughboys,” possibly because the brass buttons resembled small fried-dough pastries
or perhaps from the dust that coated infantry on the march, as if they’d been rolled in flour
Whatever the origin, the nickname stuck
legend says German soldiers called them “Devil Dogs”

steps.purpose: Notice how an honest writer marks what is uncertain.
students: Why not just say where the name came from?
Which statements on the posters have no careful word? Why?

steps.title: An epitaph, a proclamation, a promise
script: **Formal words.** Read the three short texts. The epitaph uses old, formal words: *rests*, *honored glory*, *known but to God*. Wilson’s proclamation asks for *solemn pride*. The poster’s promise speaks straight to the dead, as *you*, in three short sentences.

screen.text:
“Here rests in honored glory an American soldier known but to God”
— a grave in The Memorial

A day “filled with solemn pride in the heroism of those who died in the country’s service”
— President Woodrow Wilson, 1919

“You will not be forgotten. Your sacrifice mattered. And because of you, we live in freedom.”
— When the Guns Fell Silent
screen.cite: The Memorial and When the Guns Fell Silent

steps.purpose: Hear the formal words people choose when they remember.
students: Pick one word that sounds solemn. Why that word?
Who is spoken to in the promise?

steps.title: Choose a handout
script: Students choose a handout; every level ends with writing of their own.

levels.name: Green Level
levels.summary: Find the pattern in the six title cards. Write an *After…* sequence from a bank of facts. Find the careful words in the doughboys passage, and say which line you would keep.

levels.name: Yellow Level
levels.summary: Name the device and its effect in four lines. Analyze word choice in the epitaph, the proclamation and the promise. Then write a memorial inscription that uses one device.

levels.name: Red Level
levels.summary: Judge when careful words are needed and when they are not. Compare the two posters’ closing lines for audience and purpose. Then plan and write a short Veterans Day speech.

steps.purpose: Study the devices and use them, at the right level of challenge.
students: Choose Green, Yellow or Red. All three read the exhibition’s words, then write your own.

steps.title: Words, or silence?
script: Ask three students to read one line of their writing aloud, without comment. Then put the exhibition’s own question: *“Why might people choose silence, rather than words, to honor those who died?”* Let the room think before anyone answers.

screen.question: Why might people choose silence, rather than words, to honor those who died?

steps.purpose: Close by weighing what words can do, and what silence does.
students: Read one line you wrote today.
Is there something silence says that words cannot?

steps.title: Look back
script: Put the objectives back on the screen, asked as questions: *“Can you now…?”* Students show a thumb up, sideways or down; for the last, ask two Red Level writers to read a line of their speeches.
